summary:
What we developed: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is a story-driven game and website for kids aged 10 to 15. Players are sent to Mars in the year 2049, but their ship breaks on landing and they have 10 days to survive and get home. Junie, a shy jellyfish-astronaut, guide and teach them how to live on Mars. The website opens with a scrolling descent from Earth to the Martian surface.
How it addresses the challenge: The challenge asks for a kid-friendly way to manage a lunar or Martian outpost. Players balance oxygen, power, radiation shielding, food and communication delay, and every choice has consequences. Real NASA open data powers it: a space weather alert is based on a real DONKI solar flare event. Radiation flares are from RadLab.
Why it matters: Living off Earth is one of the biggest problems of future space exploration. By turning it into an adventure, the project helps children understand life support, energy and radiation safety, and inspires the next generation of explorers.
“Earth is the cradle of humanity, but one cannot live in a cradle forever.” — Konstantin Tsiolkovsky.
details:
What it does and how it works:

Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive mission simulator for kids aged 10-15. Players run a lunar or Martian outpost and balance the trade-offs that real mission planners face: the power grid, life support and oxygen, radiation shielding during solar storms, food production, and communication delay with Earth. Junie, a jellyfish-astronaut, guides the player. She explains each decision in simple language and shows why one choice costs something somewhere else. Space-weather events in the game are based on real NASA data, such as solar flares from DONKI and radiation levels from RadLab.

Benefits:

It teaches systems thinking. Kids see that boosting power or shielding means giving something else up.

It turns real space science into something playable, with no prior knowledge needed.

It runs in a browser, so it’s free to use in classrooms and at home with no installation.

Intended impact:

To make kids curious about space science and engineering, and to help them see that astronauts’ work is mostly careful decision-making under pressure. A flare that appears in the game is based on a real event, which links play to real NASA research.

Tools, languages and software:

HTML, Tailwind CSS (via CDN) and vanilla JavaScript, so it stays lightweight and loads quickly.

NASA open data: the DONKI API for solar flare and space-weather events, with a static fallback if the live feed is unavailable. Radiation levels and flux magnitude from RadLab using python script.

Pixel-art styling inspired by our own Mars Walker game, and our original Junie character illustration.

No special hardware is needed, only a device with a web browser.

How it’s creative:

Junie is an original character who appears at key moments, so the learning feels like a story and not a lesson.

Real solar events trigger in-game storms, so the “you must shield your crew now” moment is based on actual space weather.

Players learn by making trade-offs instead of reading facts, and there’s no single “right” answer.

Factors the team considered:

Audience: the language, visuals and difficulty suit ages 10-15.

Accuracy vs. simplicity: the science is simplified without becoming wrong.

Accessibility: it works on school computers and low-cost devices, and doesn’t depend on a live connection.

Reliability: the fallback data keeps the game working if the NASA feed is down.

Open source: the project is built to be shared and reused by educators.
